summary_responses.subtopic: Federal Credit Union Chartering & Associational Common Bond Rules
summary_responses.response: The National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) Board has issued a final rule, effective January 4, 2027, amending its criteria for determining associational common bonds under 12 CFR Part 701. Under the updated rule, requiring members to buy a good, product, or service as a condition of membership will no longer automatically bar a group from qualifying as a recognized association, eliminating an exclusion previously tied to a fraternal association example. However, the NCUA is retaining its long-standing policy that associations based primarily on a client-customer relationship remain ineligible, and the changes apply only to single associational and multiple common bond federal credit unions rather than occupational, community, or federally insured state-chartered credit unions. After reviewing feedback on its April 8, 2026 proposal—which was supported by all but one of the 18 commenters and opposed by a bankers association concerned about eroding statutory restrictions—the Board added modifications to detail client-customer review criteria, provide relevant examples, and simplify the review process for pre-approved groups. Asserting its rulemaking authority under the Federal Credit Union Act, the NCUA emphasized that evaluating the totality of a group's circumstances and maintaining oversight safeguards will protect field of membership integrity while expanding access to financial services.

summary_responses.subtopic: Federal Reserve Regulation D & Depository Institution Reserve Requirements
summary_responses.response: The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System has issued a final rule amending Regulation D to establish the annual reserve requirement exemption amount and the low reserve tranche for 2027 as required by the Federal Reserve Act. Because total reservable liabilities across all depository institutions decreased by 2.4 percent between June 30, 2025, and June 30, 2026, the reserve requirement exemption amount will remain unchanged from 2026 at $39.2 million. Although the rule becomes effective on December 18, 2026, and the updated low reserve tranche applies starting January 1, 2027, these statutory adjustments will not change actual reserve requirements, which remain at zero percent since March 2020. summary_responses.subtopic: Postal Regulatory Commission Competitive Product Rate & Filing Proceedings
summary_responses.response: On November 12, 2026, the Postal Service filed a notice with the Postal Regulatory Commission proposing rate and classification changes for Competitive products, which are scheduled to take effect on January 17, 2027. Under the proposed rates, major domestic products—including Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Parcel Select, and USPS Ground Advantage—will see an average price increase of 5.9 percent, while major international products will rise by an average of 7.9 percent alongside various increases for extra and special services. Key classification updates include a new permanent 11 percent flat fuel surcharge on those domestic packages (which will eventually adjust weekly), a 20 percent repricing fee for postage underpayments or overpayments caused by inaccurate dimensions or weight, and a new Shipping Label Noncompliance Fee. The Postal Service also plans to update Premium Forwarding Service options, add Delivered Duty Paid as an optional feature for International Priority Airmail, revise international country group assignments, and expand international flat rate price groups from 8 to 20. To evaluate whether the planned changes comply with applicable laws and regulations, the Commission established Docket No. CP2027-1, appointed Christopher Mohr as Public Representative, and invited public comments by December 4, 2026.

summary_responses.subtopic: Clearing Agency Capital Management & Securities Exchange Fee Holidays
summary_responses.response: The Securities and Exchange Commission published a notice that The Options Clearing Corporation (OCC) filed an immediately effective proposed rule change to implement a clearing fee holiday from December 1, 2026, through December 31, 2026. Under its Capital Management Policy, OCC is returning excess capital to market participants because strong 2026 clearing volumes and lower-than-budgeted margin cash interest expenses have kept its liquid net assets funded by equity (LNAFBE) above 110% of its Target Capital Requirement. The fee holiday lowers transaction clearing fees from $0.025 per contract to $0.00 and removes the $200 minimum monthly fee pending regulatory approvals, with fees reverting to the prior schedule on the first trading day of 2027. Although the measure is estimated to result in approximately $77 million in lost revenue, OCC projects that its LNAFBE will remain above its early warning thresholds for both 2026 and 2027 under realistic trading volume scenarios. OCC states that the fee holiday complies with the Exchange Act's requirement for equitable and reasonable fees, supported by ongoing Board and SEC oversight as well as regular financial transparency.

summary_responses.subtopic: Medicare Hospital Insurance Deductible & Extended Care Coinsurance Determinations
summary_responses.response: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) has issued a notice announcing the calendar year (CY) 2027 inpatient hospital deductible and coinsurance amounts for Medicare Part A, effective January 1, 2027. Calculated using statutory formulas that factor in a 2.32 percent payment-weighted average rate increase and a -0.1 percent real case-mix adjustment, the CY 2027 inpatient hospital deductible will rise from $1,736 to $1,776. Because coinsurance amounts are defined by law as fixed percentages of the deductible, daily coinsurance rates will increase to $444 for the 61st through 90th day of hospitalization, $888 for lifetime reserve days, and $222 for the 21st through 100th day of extended care in a skilled nursing facility. CMS estimates that these higher rates, combined with changes in the number of deductibles and coinsurance days paid, will increase total costs to Medicare beneficiaries by about $770 million. Additionally, CMS waived the standard proposed rulemaking and public comment process because this annual update does not establish or change a substantive legal standard and otherwise qualifies for a good cause waiver.

summary_responses.subtopic: Federal Electronic Payment Systems Modernization & Digital Fee Infrastructure
summary_responses.response: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to eliminate paper payment methods—such as cash, money orders, and paper checks—and require electronic payments instead. This proposal complies with Executive Order 14247, which aims to increase federal government efficiency by phasing out paper receipts, and aligns the FAA's regulations with its current practice of requesting payments through Pay.gov. The proposed amendments apply to payment provisions across multiple parts of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations—covering civil penalties, aircraft registration and recording, duplicate certificates and knowledge test reports, overflight fees, and FAA services performed outside the United States—while also removing paper payment references from three Advisory Circular guidance documents. Consistent with the executive order, the FAA would still allow alternative payment methods where otherwise authorized by law, and the agency estimates the rule will yield $99,815 in annual cost savings with only de minimis transition costs for customers. Public comments on the proposed rule and draft guidance revisions must be submitted on or before January 4, 2027.

summary_responses.response: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a notice of proposed rulemaking to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) affecting certain Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH Model EC135 and EC635T2+ helicopters. Prompted by a directive from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, the proposal addresses incomplete manufacturer instructions for post-hard-landing inspections, which could lead to undetected tail rotor control damage, component failure, and reduced helicopter control. If adopted, the AD would require operators to conduct a one-time inspection of the tail rotor control system within 12 months of the rule's effective date, carry out any necessary corrective actions, and revise existing aircraft maintenance manuals and inspection programs. The FAA estimates the directive would apply to 289 U.S.-registered helicopters, costing operators $340 per aircraft for the inspection and $85 per aircraft for maintenance program revisions, excluding any variable repair costs. Public comments on this proposed rulemaking must be received by the FAA by January 4, 2027.

summary_responses.subtopic: National Park Administration, Conservation & Multi-Use Trail Regulation
summary_responses.response: The National Park Service has issued a final rule, effective December 21, 2026, that amends special regulations for Mammoth Cave National Park to expand bicycle and horseback riding access. Specifically, the rule authorizes the park superintendent to designate approximately 37 miles of multi-use trails for bicycling—including eight newly constructed trails—while removing bicycle access from the White Oak Trail and closing the Maple Springs Connector Trail. It also permits equestrian use on the approximately 5.4-mile Houchin Ferry North/Ollie Road, where motor vehicle traffic is rare. These updates implement part of the selected alternative from the 2024 Comprehensive Land and River Trails Plan and Environmental Assessment, which the agency began developing in 2022 to replace outdated plans and address deteriorating trail conditions. Following a December 2024 Finding of No Significant Impact, the plan relies on sustainable trail construction techniques to limit erosion and allows the superintendent to authorize electric bicycles on trails open to traditional bicycles.
